opus-5.5.text:
Well, I should gently correct the premise there. I didn't actually study at Drexel. My undergraduate degree was in computer science at Cambridge, at Queens' College, and then much later, after my years in the games industry, I went back to do a PhD in cognitive neuroscience at UCL.

But I'm happy to talk about what I valued from that training, because the two experiences shaped me in quite different ways.

Cambridge gave me a rigorous grounding in the fundamentals of computation: algorithms, complexity, the theory of what's computable. More than any particular fact, it taught me how to think precisely about problems and break them down. It was also a place where you were surrounded by people who were extremely passionate about ideas, and that atmosphere of intellectual ambition, the sense that you could take on the biggest questions, really stayed with me.

The PhD at UCL was almost a deliberate detour. I'd always believed that if you wanted to build general intelligence, the brain is the only existence proof we have, so it made sense to study it directly. I worked on memory and imagination, looking at the hippocampus and how we construct scenes and simulate the future. What I valued there was learning the experimental mindset, careful hypothesis testing and humility in the face of data, and seeing which algorithmic ideas from neuroscience, like episodic memory and replay, might inspire AI systems.

Combining those, the engineering and computational view from Cambridge and the biological, systems-level view from neuroscience, was really the intellectual foundation for DeepMind. Breakthroughs often happen at the intersection of fields, and having training in more than one gives you a kind of stereo vision on the problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should gently correct you there, Lex. I didn't go to Drexel. My undergraduate degree was in computer science at Cambridge, at Queens' College, and then much later I did my PhD in cognitive neuroscience at UCL. So I'm not sure where Drexel came from, but I'd hate for someone there to think I'm claiming an alma mater I don't have.

But the spirit of the question is a good one, because I do think a lot about what that training gave me. Cambridge was interesting for me because I'd already been working in industry. I'd been at Bullfrog, I'd worked on Theme Park, so I came in with this very practical, build-the-thing mindset, and Cambridge is almost the opposite of that. It's deeply theoretical. You're reading Turing, you're doing the formal computation stuff, information theory, and at the time I remember being slightly impatient with it. I wanted to make things.

What I value in hindsight is exactly that friction. It gave me the rigour to think about problems from first principles rather than just hacking toward something that works. And the tutorial system, that one-on-one or two-on-one supervision where someone really grills you on your reasoning, that was formative. You can't hide behind a vague answer. It's the closest thing to the scientific method as a lived experience.

And then UCL gave me the other half, which was neuroscience. That's where the idea crystallised that you could study the brain to get inspiration for AI, that memory and imagination are actually two sides of the same process. So if I'm honest, the thing I value most is the combination. The computer science gave me the tools, and the neuroscience gave me the questions worth pointing them at.
